title: Plans: is this approach effective, and why?
blurb: Judge stage choices, planning horizon, product-based planning, estimating and tolerances in a scenario, and pick the reason that fits.
question: Brennan Mutual's project manager proposes adding a separate 'project closure' stage after decommissioning the data centres. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?

teach.h: Plans that the board can actually steer by
teach.body: Formally, the plans practice facilitates communication and control by defining the products to be delivered and the means to deliver them, to satisfy the business case. In plain English: a plan is good when it is built from the products, detailed only as far ahead as can be seen, split into stages that give the board real decision points, honest about risk, and fitted with tolerances that reflect which constraints matter most. BL4 items test exactly these choices.

teach.caption: Analysing risks runs alongside every step: a plan stays a draft until its risks have been analysed. The same technique is used for project, stage and team plans (7.3.1).

teach.body: Only the near future can be planned in detail, so PRINCE2 uses a high-level project plan and a detailed stage plan for the current stage. There are at least two stages, the first being initiation. Shorter stages give the board more control; longer stages put less burden on senior management. Stage ends can be aligned with external influences, such as budget cycles. The initiation stage plan is made in starting up; every later stage plan is prepared near the end of the stage before.

teach.caption: Closing a project happens inside stage 5, the final stage. It is never planned as a stage of its own.

rows.label: Approved by
values: Board, at authorize initiation or a stage

teach.body: Project and team managers always plan using estimates: top-down, bottom-up, comparative, parametric, data analytics or expert consensus such as Delphi or planning poker. In a linear-sequential project, product descriptions must be detailed enough to estimate cost and time with confidence. Tolerances exist for each aspect of performance at each plan level, and knowing which constraints take precedence is crucial when choosing approaches and setting tolerances.

teach.text: Classic traps: closing a project is not a stage, so closure is planned in the final stage's plan; the initiation stage plan is made in starting up, so a five-stage project needs four more stage plans, each prepared near the end of the stage before; and the project plan is created in initiation, not in starting up or at a stage boundary.

teach.body: Mairi Campbell, the project manager, builds the project plan in initiation with estimates for all five stages, so the board can confirm viability. She keeps the wave migration detail for its own stage plan, prepared near the end of the foundations stage. She uses the pilot wave's actual effort to estimate later waves, analyses the risks of the December change freeze before submitting each plan, and plans closure inside the decommissioning stage.

Test the detail: near-term detail only, but enough to estimate with confidence.
Test the stages: real decision points, sized to risk and complexity, closure in the final stage.
Test risk and tolerance: risks analysed before approval; tolerances reflect the key constraints.
Then pick the reason that explains the verdict in this scenario.
Minimum two stages; shorter stages give more control, longer ones less board burden (2.4).
Initiation stage plan in SU; later stage plans near the end of the previous stage (7.2.2.2).
Closure is planned in the final stage's plan, never as its own stage (7.2.2.2, ch 18).
Project plan in IP gives estimates so the board can confirm viability (7.2.2.1, tab 7.2).
A plan stays a draft until its risks are analysed; estimates need enough product detail (7.3.1).

summary: You can now judge whether stages, planning horizon, product-based planning, estimating and tolerances are applied effectively. You can spot the classic planning errors and choose the reason that explains them.

A.q: Brennan Mutual's Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. Project manager Mairi Campbell prepares the project plan with time and cost estimates for all five stages so that the board can decide whether the project is viable before authorizing it. Which principle is the plans practice applying, and why?
options: Manage by stages, because the project plan covers every stage of Skyline
Ensure continued business justification, because the estimates show viability
Focus on products, because the project plan is built from Skyline's products
Manage by exception, because the estimates are used to set the tolerances
A.why: The plans practice applies continued business justification by aligning the plan's targets with the business case and providing estimates on which the board can confirm viability (tab 7.2).

whyNot.0: The project plan does span the stages, but the purpose described here is confirming viability.
whyNot.2: Plans are product-based, but the stem is about estimates supporting the viability decision.
whyNot.3: Tolerances relate to manage by exception, but the stem describes estimates used to judge viability.

A.q: During initiation of Project Skyline, the products and work packages for the foundations stage have been defined. Mairi Campbell and Stratoshift's delivery lead now work out the effort and cost of each work package, using the effort recorded on similar migrations at another client as a guide. Which step of the planning technique are they applying?
options: Organizing work packages
Defining and analysing the products
Preparing the schedule
Preparing estimates
A.why: Preparing estimates sizes the effort and cost of the work; project and team managers always plan using estimates, for example comparative estimates based on similar past work (7.3.1.3).

whyNot.0: Organizing work packages groups the delivery activities, which has already been done here.
whyNot.1: Defining and analysing the products produces the PPD, PBS, product descriptions and product flow diagram, which are already in place.
whyNot.2: Scheduling sequences the work and its durations using the estimates once they exist.

A.q: Project Skyline is in initiation. Mairi Campbell's draft project plan includes a day-by-day schedule for the third migration wave, which starts about twelve months from now. What should Mairi do?
options: Keep the plan high level and detail wave 3 in its own stage plan
Keep the daily schedule so the board sees the full detail now
Move the wave 3 schedule into the initiation stage plan
Ask Stratoshift to agree the wave 3 schedule as a fixed contract
A.why: Only the near future can be planned in detail. The project plan stays high level; detailed planning happens in the stage plan prepared near the end of the previous stage (7.2.1, 7.2.2.2).

whyNot.1: Detail far beyond the planning horizon is unreliable and gives false confidence.
whyNot.2: The initiation stage plan covers initiation work only, not delivery waves a year away.
whyNot.3: Fixing detail a year ahead ignores the planning horizon and the need to plan each stage near its start.

B.q: Project Skyline has five stages: initiation, foundations, wave migration, core banking and decommissioning. Mairi Campbell produced the initiation stage plan while starting up the project. How many more stage plans will be needed, and when should they be prepared?
options: Five, including one prepared for closing the project
Four, each prepared near the end of the stage before
Four, all prepared during the initiation stage
Five, all prepared during the initiation stage
B.why: The initiation stage plan is created in starting up; each of the four later stage plans is prepared near the end of the stage before (7.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Closing a project is not a stage, so it has no stage plan of its own.
whyNot.2: Preparing all stage plans in initiation ignores the planning horizon.
whyNot.3: Initiation's own plan already exists, and later plans are prepared near each stage end.

B.q: Project Skyline's wave migration stage is eight months long and covers three waves. The chief risk officer wants independent assurance of every wave, and the board wants to decide before each wave starts whether the project should continue. Which change best fits the manage by stages guidance?
options: Ask for weekly highlight reports during the eight-month stage
Merge the waves and core banking into one longer stage
Split the stage so that each wave ends at a stage boundary
Hold the go or no-go decisions inside each team plan
B.why: Stage boundaries are the board's decision points; shorter stages give more control where risk is high (2.4, 7.2.3).

whyNot.0: Highlight reports keep the board informed, but they are not decision points for authorizing the next piece of work.
whyNot.1: A longer stage reduces board burden but gives fewer decision points, the opposite of what is needed.
whyNot.3: Team plans are optional plans for the team manager; board decisions are made at stage boundaries.

B.q: During initiation of Project Skyline, Mairi Campbell proposes adding a sixth stage called 'project closure' after the decommissioning stage, with its own stage plan. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Plan closure in the project plan instead of a stage plan
Keep the sixth stage so the board can authorize closure
Ask the business layer to plan closure after stage 5
Plan the closure work in the decommissioning stage plan
B.why: Closing a project is part of the final stage, not a stage; closure activities are planned in the final stage's plan (ch 18, fig 12.1).

whyNot.0: Closure activities still need detailed planning, and that happens in the final stage plan.
whyNot.1: The board authorizes closure in directing a project; that does not require a separate stage.
whyNot.2: Closure is run by the project manager in the final stage, not left to the business layer.

C.q: Project Skyline's foundations stage is delivered in a linear-sequential way. Mairi Campbell's product description for the cloud landing zone says only 'a secure cloud environment', and she asks Stratoshift for a firm estimate of cost and time based on it. Is this an appropriate application of the 'plans' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the PPD already sets acceptance criteria for the project
Yes, because estimates are refined later as the stage progresses
No, because product descriptions need detail to estimate with confidence
No, because the landing zone belongs in the project product description
C.why: In a linear-sequential project, product descriptions should be detailed enough to estimate cost and time with confidence (7.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: The PPD sets project-level acceptance criteria, but that does not give enough detail to estimate this product.
whyNot.1: Refining estimates later does not justify asking for a firm estimate from a one-line description.
whyNot.3: The landing zone is one of the products and needs its own product description; the PPD covers the project's major products.

C.q: Project Skyline's wave migration stage plan is ready. Mairi Campbell submits it for approval before analysing the risks from the December change freeze and month-end restrictions, planning to analyse them after the board approves it. Is this an appropriate application of the 'plans' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because stage plans are prepared near the end of the stage before
Yes, because the risk register already exists from initiation
No, because a plan stays a draft until its risks have been analysed
No, because risk analysis is the risk owner's job, not the PM's
C.why: Analysing risks runs alongside the planning steps, and a plan remains a draft until its risks have been addressed (7.3.1).

whyNot.0: It is true that stage plans are prepared near the end of the previous stage, but that does not explain approving one before its risks are analysed.
whyNot.1: The risk register exists, but the plan's own risks still need analysing before approval.
whyNot.3: Risk owners respond to risks; analysing a plan's risks is part of the PM's planning technique.

C.q: Brennan Mutual has a December change freeze during which no migrations may happen. Mairi Campbell sets the end of the wave migration stage to fall just before the freeze, so the board's review takes place while no migration work can run anyway. How well does this apply the 'plans' practice, and why?
options: Well, because stage ends can be aligned with external influences
Well, because shorter stages give the project board more control
Poorly, because all stages should be planned to the same length
Poorly, because stage ends are set by the team managers' schedules
C.why: Stage ends can be aligned with external influences, such as the business's calendar, so their effect is clear and decisions fall at sensible points (2.4, 7.2.3).

whyNot.1: It is true shorter stages give more control, but the stage is not being shortened; the reason is the alignment with the freeze.
whyNot.2: Stage length depends on risk, complexity and decision points, not a rule of equal length.
whyNot.3: The project manager decides how stages are applied, with the board approving plans (tab 7.1); team schedules do not set stage boundaries.

reteach.title: Plan like a satnav, not a printed map
reteach.question: Why would a satnav that recalculates at junctions beat a printed route planned a year ago?

blocks.body: A printed route planned a year ahead is detailed but wrong by the time you drive it. A satnav shows the whole journey in outline and gives precise turns only for the next few miles, recalculating at junctions. PRINCE2 plans work the same way: an outline project plan, a detailed plan for the current stage, and a fresh stage plan near each stage end, which is the board's junction to decide whether to carry on.

blocks.h: When each Skyline plan is made

blocks.text: More detail is not better planning. Detail beyond the planning horizon, or a plan approved before its risks are analysed, is weaker than a well-scoped outline.

explain.body: Define and analyse products (PPD, PBS, product descriptions, PFD); organize work packages with no overlaps or gaps; prepare estimates; prepare the schedule; prepare the budget; document the plan; analyse risks throughout.

test.q: Mairi Campbell groups Project Skyline's migration activities into work packages for Stratoshift and the in-house team, checking that no application appears in two work packages and none is missed. Which step is this?
options: Preparing the schedule
Organizing work packages
Preparing estimates
Documenting the plan
test.why: Organizing work packages groups delivery activities so there is no overlap in scope between work packages and no gaps (7.3.1.2).

whyNot.0: Scheduling sequences the work after it is packaged.
whyNot.3: Documenting writes up the plan narrative.

explain.body: At least two stages, the first being initiation. Detail only to the planning horizon. Initiation stage plan in starting up; later stage plans near the end of the stage before; closure inside the final stage.

test.q: A small Brennan Mutual project to replace branch printers has a few well-understood products and a mature delivery method. What is the minimum number of stages it needs?
options: One
Three
Two
Four
test.why: Every PRINCE2 project has at least two stages: initiation plus at least one delivery stage (2.4, 7.2.3.1).

whyNot.0: Initiation is always a stage, so one stage is not enough.
whyNot.1: Three is allowed but not the minimum.
whyNot.3: Four is more than needed for a simple project.

explain.body: Estimating methods include top-down, bottom-up, comparative, parametric, data analytics and expert consensus. The budget covers activity costs and may include a risk budget for risk responses and a change budget for approved changes.

test.q: Mairi Campbell wants money set aside in Project Skyline's budget to pay for a pre-planned rollback if a migration wave fails. What should this money be?
options: A change budget
A cost tolerance
A benefits tolerance
A risk budget
test.why: A risk budget funds specific responses to risks, such as contingent plans (7.3.1; risk budget, risk practice ch 9).

whyNot.0: A change budget funds approved requests for change.
whyNot.1: Cost tolerance is a permitted deviation, not money set aside for a response.

explain.body: Tolerances exist at each plan level for the aspects of performance. Understanding which constraints take precedence is crucial to choosing approaches and setting tolerances. The project plan in initiation gives the board estimates to confirm viability.

test.q: Brennan Mutual's board has a very low appetite for outages and a moderate appetite for cost risk, and the lease end date cannot move. Why should Mairi Campbell establish which of these takes precedence before setting tolerances?
options: It shapes the delivery approach and the tolerances set
It replaces the need for a risk management approach
It decides how many work packages the stage needs
It fixes the number of stages in the project plan
test.why: Understanding which constraints take precedence is crucial to choosing the approach and setting tolerances (7.2.4).

whyNot.1: A risk management approach is still needed.
whyNot.2: Work package numbers come from organizing the work, not from constraint priority.
whyNot.3: Stage numbers depend on decision points, risk and complexity.
